opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, that's the question that gets me most excited, because "physical limits" is where the interesting engineering starts.

The way I think about it, MRC was never about squeezing a little more out of any single link. Copper and optics are both getting closer to what physics will allow per lane, and you can't wish that away. What you *can* do is stop treating the network as a set of individual paths and treat it as a fabric. If you can spread traffic intelligently across many paths, react quickly when one gets congested or fails, and recover without the whole job stalling, then your scaling story depends much less on any one wire being perfect.

That's the core bet: as individual components hit their ceilings, the leverage moves up the stack, into how you route, how you handle loss, and how tightly the transport cooperates with the hardware underneath it. At very large scale, failures aren't edge cases. Something is always flapping somewhere. A protocol that assumes the network is imperfect and is built to tolerate that gracefully scales much better than one that needs everything to go right.

I don't want to pretend there's no ceiling. Eventually you're bounded by power, by the speed of light across a building or a campus, and by how many ports you can physically fit and cool. Nothing we do in software repeals any of that. But I think we're a long way from the point where the protocol is the bottleneck. In the near term, the bigger question is co-design: getting the people building the chips, the optics, the switches, and the transport layer to treat it as one system. When that happens, you find a lot of headroom you didn't know you had.

So I'm optimistic, but in a specific way. Not "we'll keep doubling forever," more "we're nowhere near done figuring out how to use the physics we already have."

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's really the central question, and I think the honest answer is that the physical limits are real, but they're not where most people think they are.

When people talk about hitting the wall, they're usually thinking about electrical signaling. Copper over a backplane, SerDes rates, the energy per bit you burn just moving data a few centimeters. And they're right that those are getting tight. Every doubling of lane rate costs you reach, costs you power, costs you signal integrity headroom. We're already at a point where a big fraction of the power in a rack isn't compute, it's just moving bits around.

The way I think about MRC's scaling story is that it was never designed around a single fabric getting faster. It was designed around the assumption that the bottleneck is going to keep shifting. So instead of one monolithic network that has to do everything, you have multiple rails, each one tuned for a particular class of traffic, and the scheduling layer is aware of what's underneath it. That means when one rail hits its physical ceiling, you don't have to rip out the whole architecture. You add rails, or you swap the medium on one of them, and the abstraction above it stays stable.

Where that gets interesting is optics. Once you're talking about moving to co-packaged optics or even just shorter electrical reaches with optical interconnect beyond that, the question becomes less about raw bandwidth and more about the economics and reliability of the transceivers. Optics scale beautifully on distance and bandwidth density, but every laser is a failure point, and at the scale we're talking about you're not asking whether a component will fail, you're asking how many fail per hour. So the architecture has to treat link failure as a steady-state condition, not an exception. MRC does that reasonably well because the multi-rail design gives you redundancy as a byproduct rather than as an add-on.

The limit I actually worry about more is latency. Bandwidth you can keep buying, within reason. But the speed of light doesn't negotiate, and as these clusters physically get bigger, the round trip across the system starts to matter for the collective operations that training depends on. You can't fix that with a faster transceiver. You fix it by being smarter about placement, about which communication patterns actually need to span the whole machine versus which can be kept local, and by co-designing the workload with the topology instead of pretending the network is a flat, infinitely fast thing.

So, can it scale? I think yes, probably further than the skeptics expect, but not by brute force. It scales by being honest about the physics and pushing the complexity into the places where you still have degrees of freedom, which these days is mostly the software and the topology, not the wire.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is distinguishing between scaling the network and making better use of the network you have. MRC can help with the second, but it doesn’t remove the physical limits. You still have finite bandwidth, propagation delay, and power constraints.

As you approach those limits, the question becomes: can you keep communication balanced and avoid having one congested path hold up the whole job? To the extent MRC does that, it can help you get closer to the capacity you’ve already built. But I wouldn’t expect that benefit to continue indefinitely. Eventually, further scaling requires changes to the hardware, the topology, or how much communication the workload needs.

sol-6.1.text: I think the key is that MRC has to scale within those physical constraints. You can’t assume bandwidth will keep increasing or latency will keep falling indefinitely. The question becomes how much useful work you can get out of the network you have—how efficiently you communicate, where you place computation, and how much data actually needs to move. Those improvements can create room to grow, but they don’t eliminate the underlying limits.
